extracted.intended_audience: legislators, agency officials, administrative law practitioners, and policy-makers responsible for rule-making and adjudicative procedures in administrative agencies
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and recommended procedural rules for administrative agencies to ensure fair participation: notice, opportunities to communicate, evidentiary rules, access to information, representation, impartiality, and reasons for decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice: individualized versus general notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A person entitled to participate in a rule-making proceeding may be sufficiently identifiable and sufficiently affected by its outcome to be entitled to receive a personalized notice; otherwise notice may take the form of a general public announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High level of particularity may be demanded in some cases (case law cited). Example: pay TV licensees could be entitled to individual notice because they are easily identifiable and small in number. Authorities cited emphasize that notices in general terms can be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participants' right to communicate information and views
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who are sufficiently interested to receive notice must be accorded standing as 'participants' and should have a reasonable opportunity to communicate information and views to the agency and to comment on submissions of other participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information that may influence the agency's decision should be subject to critical examination by all participants, with reasonable consideration for confidentiality. This right does not automatically require formal hearings or oral presentations; the opportunity must be reasonable in the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible modes and scope of participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different situations require different choices about who should participate and what the scope and modes of participation should be; the standard emphasizes function rather than prescribing a single method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every participant must have equal opportunities; consolidation of interventions can be warranted depending on subject-matter and character of proceedings. Agencies should be encouraged to experiment with innovative methods of obtaining information and views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of fact-collection and hearing authority (with safeguards)
rubrics_metrics.description: The task of collecting information sometimes may be delegated (to panels, single members, staff, or external hearing officers), and in some models delegates may exercise decision-making power subject to agency review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each delegation model raises concerns about who makes the effective decision, collegiality, and whether sufficient safeguards are extended to participants. Delegation should be considered where time, geography and caseloads impose constraints; study and recommendations on feasibility/scope are advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary latitude for administrative agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should be allowed wide evidentiary latitude and, except where otherwise prescribed by statute, should not be required to follow the rules of evidence that apply in courts of law, other than rules of evidentiary privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many courtroom rules of evidence are unsuited to agency work; rules of evidence should be developed as incidents of administrative procedure. Model rules of evidence in the recommended format would be useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish agency procedures and provide procedural information
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing a reasonable opportunity to participate implies agencies must provide interested persons with reasonable access to information about agency procedures, in large part by formally adopting and publishing their procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all procedures can be formalized; agencies should supplement formal rules with oral or written elaborations of informal procedural requirements or interpretive rulings, and should provide assistance in completion of forms. These services can aid participants without imposing undue burden on staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on agency assistance to participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency personnel should not, as a standard practice, make applications on behalf of persons or act in an advisory capacity; assistance should be limited to supplementary information and relatively minor help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More extensive or formal assistance should be provided only if the agency's enabling Act expressly authorizes it, because acting as advisor/agent raises legal problems (liability, appearance of bias). Other non-staff forms of assistance (e.g., specialized advocates) may be contemplated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing professional representation (including non-lawyers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A participant should be allowed to employ a professional representative in a proceeding, going beyond the traditional 'right to counsel' to include non-lawyers whose specialized abilities may assist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain roles (handling sensitive/confidential information) may require qualified legal professionals; in other cases accountants, engineers, scientists, administrators etc. may play representative roles. Examples: customs agents, members of veterans' groups, Bureau of Pensions Advocates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to information relevant to the proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants should have reasonable access to all information that is relevant to the decision the agency will make and should not have to rely on the public Access to Information Act procedures to obtain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open access contributes to fairness, efficiency and accountability and enables participants to help the decision-maker reach the 'right' decision. Access should be broader than what is mandated for the general public under general access statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality should be the exception; protective mechanisms for sensitive information
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain information needs confidentiality (trade secrets, psychiatric info, national security), but confidentiality should be exceptional and agencies should search for innovative ways to reconcile confidentiality with disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical mechanisms include deletion/redaction of confidential aspects and disclosure to counsel on condition of non-disclosure to parties. Such arrangements may strain solicitor-client relationships but can be practical compromises to obtain necessary information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of staff studies and internal opinions relevant to proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Information and opinions contained in staff studies that are relevant to a proceeding should be made available to participants, either by allowing access to the study or by ensuring the information and opinions are otherwise placed on the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should avoid 'hidden agendas' and ensure the record discloses all essential information and issues. Where a study was not produced, the agency must satisfy itself that the relevant contents have been disclosed by other means; at minimum studies should be made available to counsel for comparison with the record and reasons for decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between background studies and deliberative memoranda
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between staff studies prepared before or during a proceeding to provide background and memoranda developed to assist the agency in coming to its decision; the latter are more closely tied to deliberative process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law has been uneven about disclosure of such materials. Agencies are entitled to professional advice and assistance, and non-disclosure of strictly deliberative internal memoranda may be defensible so long as no new information or opinions are introduced that affect the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness about intergovernmental communications that influence decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter-agency and departmental contacts and private exchanges, while sometimes occurring outside a particular proceeding, can influence an agency's approach and deserve greater openness where they bear on substantive decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalizing all informal communications is neither desirable nor possible, but agencies and departments should be encouraged to intervene openly in each other's proceedings and to increase formality in communications that directly affect substantive decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining impartiality and the appearance of fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency members must be impartial in carrying out their duties and must be seen by participants and the public to be fair and impartial among those whose needs, rights and interests are at stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard applies equally to rule-making and decision-making; only where a statutory objective rationally demands a partisan orientation should departures be considered, and then only to the extent required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-of-interest rules including divestment
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict-of-interest rules for independent administrative agencies should, as a general approach, require divestment: a member should divest, at the earliest reasonable opportunity after appointment, all financial interests in matters the agency may decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule should prohibit voluntary acquisition of such interests after appointment and require divestment of interests acquired by gift or inheritance. Divestment may be limited to assets related to the agency's area. Skepticism expressed about reliance on frozen/blind trusts as adequate safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of family interests and withdrawal from matters
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency member who is aware that a spouse or close relative has a financial interest in any matter the agency may decide should publicly disclose that fact and withdraw from any file giving rise to a conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility for appointment should not depend on spouses' or relatives' divestment, but rules should account for those situations and provide for withdrawal and replacement where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforceability and remedial approach to conflict breaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Breach of conflict-of-interest requirements should be enforceable judicially by any sufficiently interested person; violation should not automatically vitiate all decisions made while the member unlawfully held office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions should be challengeable on a case-by-case basis where bias or apprehension of bias can be established. The conflict rule should not be used merely as an instrument of delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule against bias and procedures on disclosure and disqualification in proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: No agency member should sit in a proceeding in which he is interested, or is perceived to be interested, financially, personally or otherwise; the member must disclose circumstances giving rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias and withdraw unless participants consent and no conflict-of-interest rule is violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provision should be made for replacement or appointment of ad hoc members if withdrawal would reduce membership below quorum. The common law rule against bias has long been applied to administrative adjudicative functions and remains a basis to attack validity of proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving reasons for decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should be required to give reasons for each decision to encourage careful thought about facts, issues and effects, to ensure decisions are congruent with the record, and to increase the appearance of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing reasons assists in elaboration of agency policy, promotes coherence and consistency, aids identification of legislative or policy difficulties, facilitates rights of review or appeal, and supports parliamentary accountability.
